title: League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature (LWV 1)
description: Whether the district court abused its discretion in refusing to stay its order permanently enjoining the use of H.B. 2004, the 2021 Congressional Map, because the court's ordered remedial process doesn't require compliance with all of Proposition 4.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Legislative Defendants had other plain, speedy, or adequate remedies available and that the district court's denial of the stay was not an abuse of discretion.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the district court abused its discretion by refusing to stay its injunction on the Congressional Map, contending that the remedial process did not fully comply with Proposition 4 and that no other adequate remedy was available.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Legislative Defendants' petition for extraordinary relief, concluding that they had not demonstrated that the district court abused its discretion in denying the stay of its injunctive order.

title: University of Utah v. Tullis
description: Whether Condemarin v. University Hospital, 775 P.2d 348 (Utah 1989), resolves whether the 2017 GIA's damages cap-codified at Utah Code section 63G-7-604(1)(a)-violates the Utah Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Tullises argued that the 2017 GIA's damages cap is unconstitutional as applied to the University, relying on Condemarin as controlling precedent.
defendant_argument: The University argued that Condemarin is not controlling precedent because it was a plurality decision, the relevant statutes were repealed and amended, and Condemarin improperly shifted the presumption of constitutionality.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Condemarin's holding does not control in this case, reversing the district court's denial of the University's motion for partial summary judgment and remanding for further proceedings.

title: State v. Labrum
description: Whether the Utah Constitution's Due Process Clause prohibits the State from refiling criminal charges after a magistrate judge has once found insufficient evidence to bind a defendant over for trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the magistrate erred in prohibiting the refiling of rape charges, contending its initial failure to present all theories was an innocent mistake and that the Due Process Clause does not bar refiling under the clarified standard.
defendant_argument: Labrum argued that the State's refiling of rape charges was prohibited by the Due Process Clause, constituted harassment, and lacked good cause, especially due to the State's delayed presentation of legal theories.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the district court's order dismissing the charges and remanded the case for re-evaluation under a clarified legal standard, meaning the State may proceed with a second preliminary hearing if it can show no bad faith.

title: State v. Rippey
description: Whether the Plea Withdrawal Statute (PWS), specifically subsections (2)(b) and (2)(c), is constitutional under the Utah Constitution's separation of powers principles.
plaintiff_argument: Rippey argued that subsections (2)(b) and (2)(c) of the PWS are unconstitutional because they violate the separation of powers and his federal and state constitutional rights by dictating procedural rules that are the judiciary's prerogative.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the PWS is constitutional, contending that subsection (2)(b) is substantive and within the legislature's authority to regulate jurisdiction, and that the procedural components are inextricably intertwined with substantive rights.
decision_outcome: The court held that subsection (2)(b) and the waiver component of subsection (2)(c) of the Plea Withdrawal Statute were unconstitutionally enacted, violating the separation of powers under the Utah Constitution.

title: League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature (LWV 2)
description: Whether Amendment D was properly submitted to the voters with an accurate ballot title and published in newspapers for two months preceding the election as required by the Utah Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Amendment D's ballot title was misleading and inaccurate, failing to disclose its true impact on constitutional rights, and that the Legislature failed to publish the amendment in newspapers for two months as constitutionally required.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the ballot language was not misleading, that it had adequately publicized Amendment D through various online and print media, and that it had substantially complied with constitutional publication requirements.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's preliminary injunction, declaring Amendment D void and ordering that any votes cast for or against it not be counted.

title: Jenkins v. Beaver County
description: Whether ballots that were mailed before election day but not postmarked by the deadline, due to variations in United States Postal Service practices, should be accepted and counted, or if the statutory postmark requirement is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Colby Jenkins argued that many ballots were mailed before election day but not postmarked by the deadline due to USPS processing variations, and that the statutory postmark requirement is unconstitutional because it results in differential treatment of voters and interferes with the fundamental right to vote.
defendant_argument: The Lieutenant Governor and counties implicitly argued that the statutory postmark requirement is constitutional and that Mr. Jenkins failed to meet his burden of demonstrating otherwise, also questioning his third-party standing.
decision_outcome: The court denied Colby Jenkins's petition for extraordinary relief, ruling that he failed to adequately brief his constitutional challenges and did not demonstrate entitlement to the relief sought.

title: State v. Baugh
description: Whether Brevan Bringhurst Baugh's counsel provided ineffective assistance by failing to request more specific jury unanimity instructions, with the State arguing counsel's performance was reasonable and Baugh arguing it was deficient and prejudiced him.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Baugh's counsel's performance was reasonable given ambiguous caselaw and that Baugh was not prejudiced by the lack of specific unanimity instructions.
defendant_argument: Baugh argued his counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request jury instructions that would ensure a unanimous verdict on each element of the convicted count.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, vacating Baugh's conviction due to ineffective assistance of counsel.

title: Sports Medicine Research & Testing Lab. v. Board of Equalization of Salt Lake County
description: Whether Sports Medicine Research and Testing Laboratory's property is used exclusively for charitable purposes, thus qualifying for a property tax exemption under the Utah Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Sports Medicine argued its property is used for charitable purposes, citing discounted testing for government/charitable organizations, that market-rate testing for professional athletes is necessary to sustain its philanthropic mission and generate data, and that vacant space is for future charitable expansion.
defendant_argument: The Board of Equalization and Tax Commission argued that Sports Medicine's market-rate testing for professional sports leagues generates significant profit and therefore the property is not used exclusively for charitable purposes.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Tax Commission's denial of Sports Medicine's request for a property tax exemption, ruling that the property was not used exclusively for charitable purposes.

title: Bingham v. Gourley
description: Whether the Utah Health Care Malpractice Act's four-year statute of repose is unconstitutional, with the plaintiff arguing it violates the Open Courts Clause, Uniform Operation of Laws Provision, and Equal Protection Clause by denying a remedy for undiscoverable injuries, and the defendants arguing it is constitutional and violates none of these provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff contends that the Malpractice Act's four-year statute of repose is unconstitutional because it violates the Utah Constitution's Open Courts Clause, Uniform Operation of Laws Provision, and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by barring claims for injuries not discovered within the repose period.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the statute of repose is constitutional and does not violate the Open Courts Clause, Uniform Operation of Laws Provision, or the Equal Protection Clause, as it is a reasonable means to address a social and economic evil in the healthcare industry.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Bingham's claim, concluding that the Utah Health Care Malpractice Act's four-year statute of repose is constitutional and does not violate the challenged provisions.

title: Salt Lake County v. Utah State Tax Commission
description: Whether the Aircraft Valuation Law, as applied to Delta Air Lines' aircraft, resulted in an assessment below fair market value in violation of the Utah Constitution, and whether the law facially violates article XIII, section 6 of the Utah Constitution by divesting the Commission of its assessment power.
plaintiff_argument: Salt Lake County argued that the Aircraft Valuation Law, as applied, undervalued Delta's aircraft below fair market value, violating Utah Const. art. XIII, § 2, and that the law is facially unconstitutional by stripping the Tax Commission of its original assessment authority over airline property, violating Utah Const. art. XIII, § 6.
defendant_argument: The Utah State Tax Commission and Delta Air Lines argued that the Aircraft Valuation Law was correctly applied, the valuation reasonably reflected fair market value, and the County failed to provide clear and convincing evidence to the contrary or to show the law was facially unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Utah State Tax Commission's decision, ruling that Salt Lake County failed to prove the Aircraft Valuation Law was unconstitutional either as applied or on its face.

title: Kell v. State
description: Whether the district court erred in dismissing Troy Michael Kell's second petition for post-conviction relief based on time and procedural bars, and whether applying these bars violates his constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: Kell argued that the PCRA's time and procedural bars should not apply because his delay was due to ineffective assistance of initial post-conviction counsel, and applying these bars violates his rights under the Suspension Clause, Due Process Clause, and Open Courts Clause of the Utah Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the district court correctly dismissed Kell's petition because his arguments do not overcome his five-and-a-half-year delay in bringing the claim after discovering the alleged improper communication between the trial judge and jurors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment and dismissal of Kell's second petition for post-conviction relief.

title: State v. Barnett
description: Whether the Utah Constitution's Bail Provision prohibits judges from granting bail to defendants charged with a felony while on probation, or merely removes the guarantee of bail while still allowing judicial discretion.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that article I, section 8(1) of the Utah Constitution mandates that a judge deny bail to a defendant charged with a felony if that defendant is already serving probation on a felony conviction.
defendant_argument: Barnett argued that the phrase "shall be bailable except" means that while a person charged with a felony on probation is not guaranteed bail, a district court still retains discretion to grant it.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that the Bail Provision's plain language and historical understanding support the interpretation that judges retain discretion to grant bail even in cases where bail is not constitutionally guaranteed.

title: Lord v. Salt Lake County Clerk
description: Whether a property tax increase approved by a school district is subject to a referendum under the Utah Constitution or relevant statutes.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that a school district's property tax increase should be subject to a referendum, citing constitutional provisions and case law, and attempting to characterize school districts as 'subjurisdictions' to fit existing legal frameworks.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that school districts are not explicitly included in the constitutional or statutory provisions allowing referenda for counties, cities, or towns, suggesting this omission was intentional.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition for extraordinary relief, ruling that the petitioners failed to demonstrate that a school district's tax increase is subject to a referendum under current law.

title: State v. Soto
description: Whether improper contact between court personnel and a jury during trial triggers a rebuttable presumption of prejudice against the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the court of appeals incorrectly held that the conduct triggered a rebuttable presumption of prejudice, asserting that the individuals involved were not 'court participants' and that the contacts were harmless.
defendant_argument: Soto argued that he was denied his constitutional right to a fair and impartial jury due to improper juror contact, which triggered a rebuttable presumption of prejudice that the State had not rebutted.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Soto was entitled to a rebuttable presumption of prejudice due to the improper jury contact and remanded the case to the district court to determine if the State can prove harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt; if not, Soto must be given a new trial.

title: Salt Lake City Corp. v. Utah Inland Port Authority
description: Whether the Utah Inland Port Authority Act's provisions, specifically those related to zoning and tax revenue, violate the Uniform Operation of Laws Clause and Ripper Clause of the Utah Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Salt Lake City argued the Act unconstitutionally singles out three municipalities for disparate treatment and improperly delegates municipal functions and interferes with municipal money.
defendant_argument: UIPA and the State argued the Act's provisions are constitutional, being rationally related to a legitimate legislative purpose and constituting direct legislative mandates rather than improper delegations.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of Salt Lake City's challenges to the zoning provisions of the Act, finding them constitutional, but declined to rule on the tax provisions, retaining jurisdiction for further briefing due to recent amendments that may have rendered those claims moot.

title: Laws v. Grayeyes
description: Whether Willie Grayeyes was eligible to serve as county commissioner based on residency requirements.
plaintiff_argument: Kelly Laws argued that Willie Grayeyes was not a resident of San Juan County and therefore ineligible to serve as county commissioner.
defendant_argument: Willie Grayeyes argued that he was a resident of San Juan County and eligible to serve, and that Kelly Laws lacked standing to challenge his election.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Kelly Laws's challenge for lack of standing, concluding he had not alleged a sufficiently particularized injury, and affirmed the district court's denial of attorney fees to Willie Grayeyes.

title: Patterson v. State
description: Whether the Post-Conviction Remedies Act's (PCRA) time-bar provisions are constitutional and whether they unconstitutionally limit the courts' inherent writ authority to hear untimely post-conviction relief petitions.
plaintiff_argument: Patterson argued that the PCRA's time limitations should be tolled due to ineffective assistance of counsel and lack of access to courts, or that he could invoke the court's Constitutional writ power outside the PCRA, asserting the PCRA is unconstitutional if it limits the court's writ authority. He also claimed two of his claims were timely based on newly discovered evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Patterson's petition was time-barred by the PCRA, that his counsel's advice could not be imputed to the State to toll the statute, and that the PCRA wholly regulates the court's authority to issue extraordinary writs.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of most of Patterson's post-conviction relief claims as time-barred under the PCRA, finding that Patterson failed to demonstrate the time-bars violated his constitutional rights, but remanded two claims based on newly discovered evidence for further consideration.

title: In re Childers-Gray
description: Whether individuals have a common-law right to change their legal sex designations to reflect their gender identity, and whether Utah courts have the authority to adjudicate such petitions.
plaintiff_argument: Individuals have a common-law right to change their legal sex designation to align with their gender identity, and courts have the authority to grant these petitions.
defendant_argument: Changing legal sex designations is a legislative prerogative, not a judicial one, as there is no statute providing standards or procedures, making it a nonjusticiable political question, and granting such petitions would affect the rights of others.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's decision and remanded with instructions to grant the sex-change petitions.

title: Feldman v. Salt Lake City Corp.
description: Whether the Limitations on Landowner Liability Act bars wrongful death claims, whether the Act violates the Utah Constitution if it bars such claims, and whether the plaintiff's complaint sufficiently alleged that the death was not caused by an inherent risk under the Act.
plaintiff_argument: The Feldmans argued that the Act does not bar wrongful death claims, or if it does, it violates the Utah Constitution, and that their complaint sufficiently alleged Ms. Feldman's death was not caused by an inherent risk of entering the creek.
defendant_argument: Salt Lake City Corporation argued that the Act bars wrongful death claims, is constitutional, and that Ms. Feldman's death was caused by an inherent risk of entering the creek, justifying dismissal.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's dismissal of the wrongful death claims and remanded the case for further proceedings, finding that while the Act can bar such claims and is constitutional, the plaintiffs sufficiently alleged the death was not caused by an inherent risk.
